warmup.q: data class Cart(val id: String, val skus: MutableList<String>). You run val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2") and then c2.skus += "sku-2". What happens to c1.skus?
options: It now contains sku-2 too, because both carts share one list
It throws, because data class properties are immutable
It depends on whether c1 was declared with val
warmup.why: copy() is shallow. It copies the reference to the list, not the list, so c1 and c2 hold the same MutableList. val only stops you from pointing the property at another list; it says nothing about the list's contents. Records in Java behave the same way.

sections.h: Named and default arguments replace most builders
sections.html:
A builder exists to fix the telescoping constructor: one constructor per combination of optional parameters, and call sites full of unlabeled literals.

Java
new ChargeRequest(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42", null, null, true, 2, 30_000);   // which one is the timeout?
Kotlin
ChargeRequest(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42", null, null, true, 2, 30_000)         // Kotlin allows the same mess

The Java fix is the builder from Effective Java item 2: a mutable helper class with one method per field and a build() at the end. It works, and it costs you a second class that repeats every field.

Kotlin removes the problem in the language. Parameters can have defaults, and callers can name them:

Java
// Java has no named or default arguments: the record keeps the rules, a builder supplies the defaults
record ChargeRequest(long amountMinor, String currency, String token, String description,
                     boolean capture, int maxRetries, long timeoutMs) {
    ChargeRequest {
        if (maxRetries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("maxRetries must be >= 0");
    }
    ChargeRequest withTimeoutMs(long ms) {
        return new ChargeRequest(amountMinor, currency, token, description, capture, maxRetries, ms);
    }
}

var req = ChargeRequest.builder(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42").maxRetries(2).build();   // the builder: next section
var slower = req.withTimeoutMs(30_000);
Kotlin
data class ChargeRequest(
    val amountMinor: Long,
    val currency: String,
    val token: String,
    val description: String? = null,
    val capture: Boolean = true,
    val maxRetries: Int = 0,
    val timeoutMs: Long = 10_000,
) {
    init { require(maxRetries >= 0) { "maxRetries must be >= 0" } }
}

val req = ChargeRequest(amountMinor = 1_250, currency = "EUR", token = "tok_42", maxRetries = 2)
val slower = req.copy(timeoutMs = 30_000)

In the Kotlin version, every argument at the call site says what it is. Optional ones can be skipped, in any order. copy gives you a changed copy for free. And the init block runs for every construction, copy included, so nobody can skip the validation. That covers what most Java builders do.

Java callers are the gap. Java has no named arguments, so they see one constructor with seven parameters. @JvmOverloads on the constructor generates the telescoping overloads for them (one per trailing default), which is better than nothing and worse than a builder. If a Java team will call the class a lot, give them a real builder.

A rule of thumb for porting: if every call site of a Java builder sets two or three fields and leaves the rest at their defaults, the Kotlin version is a data class with defaults and nothing else. If call sites build the object across a loop or an if, keep a builder, as the next section explains.

Effective Java 3e source, item 2: the Builder

sections.h: When a builder still earns its place
sections.html:
Builders still win in four cases. The first is Java callers, as above. The second is validation that needs the whole object: "a statement descriptor is at most 22 characters, and only when capture is true" relates two fields. The third is construction spread across steps, such as headers added in a loop or 3-D Secure data added only for some cards; Kotlin's buildList { } and buildString { } are standard-library builders for exactly this. The fourth is nested data, which gets its own section next.

The modern Java shape is a record that validates plus a small builder that only collects:

Java
record IssuerCall(String url, String method, Map<String, String> headers, Duration timeout, int maxRetries) {
    IssuerCall {                                 // compact constructor: runs on every path
        Objects.requireNonNull(url, "url");
        headers = Map.copyOf(headers);           // immutable, and a copy
        if (maxRetries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("maxRetries must be >= 0");
    }
    IssuerCall withTimeout(Duration t) { return new IssuerCall(url, method, headers, t, maxRetries); }
    static Builder builder(String url) { return new Builder(url); }
    // Builder: fields with defaults, one setter each, and build() calls the constructor
}
Kotlin
data class IssuerCall(
    val url: String,
    val method: String = "GET",
    val headers: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(),
    val timeout: Duration = Duration.ofSeconds(2),
    val maxRetries: Int = 0,
) {
    init { require(maxRetries >= 0) { "maxRetries must be >= 0" } }   // runs on every path, copy() too
}
// no builder and no withers: named arguments and copy(timeout = ...) do both jobs

The builder holds no rules. The rules live in the compact constructor, which build(), the wither withTimeout and a direct new IssuerCall(...) all go through. Withers are how you get Prototype on a record: Java has no with syntax, so you write one small method per field you want to change. The Kotlin twin needs neither builder nor withers, and its init block plays the role of the compact constructor.

The JDK's newer APIs follow the same idea of a builder that produces an immutable result: HttpClient.newBuilder(), and Thread.ofVirtual(), which returns a Thread.Builder.

One builder bug deserves a name. If build() validates but the class also has a public constructor that doesn't, half the code base skips the rules. Put the rules in the type, never only in the builder.

try.title: Find where the rules live
steps: Run RecordBuilderDemo with the command below and read the four lines.
In the Java main, change .maxRetries(2) to .maxRetries(-1) (in Kotlin, maxRetries = -1). Predict: which line throws, and from where? Run it.

code.title: RecordBuilderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Objects; /** A record with a small builder: the record validates, the builder only collects. */ public class RecordBuilderDemo { record IssuerCall(String url, String method, Map<String, String> headers, Duration timeout, int maxRetries) { IssuerCall { // every path to an IssuerCall runs this Objects.requireNonNull(url, "url"); headers = Map.copyOf(headers); // really immutable if (maxRetries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("maxRetries must be >= 0, was " + maxRetries); } IssuerCall withTimeout(Duration t) { // a hand-written "wither" return new IssuerCall(url, method, headers, t, maxRetries); } IssuerCall withMaxRetries(int n) { return new IssuerCall(url, method, headers, timeout, n); } static Builder builder(String url) { return new Builder(url); } static final class Builder { private final String url; private String method = "GET"; private final Map<String, String> headers = new LinkedHashMap<>(); private Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(2); private int maxRetries = 0; private Builder(String url) { this.url = url; } Builder method(String m) { method = m; return this; } Builder header(String k, String v) { headers.put(k, v); return this; } Builder timeout(Duration t) { timeout = t; return this; } Builder maxRetries(int n) { maxRetries = n; return this; } IssuerCall build() { return new IssuerCall(url, method, headers, timeout, maxRetries); } } } public static void main(String[] args) { IssuerCall call = IssuerCall.builder("https://issuer.example/authorize") .method("POST") .header("Idempotency-Key", "auth-7731") .maxRetries(2) .build(); System.out.println("built: " + call); System.out.println("faster copy: " + call.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(800)).timeout()); try { call.headers().put("X-Debug", "1"); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("headers: unmodifiable"); } try { call.withMaxRetries(-1); // the wither can't skip validation either } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("wither: " + e.getMessage()); } } }

alt.title: RecordBuilderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l03 import java.time.Duration // The Kotlin twin of RecordBuilderDemo.java: no builder and no withers, because named arguments, // defaults and copy() do both jobs. The rules still live in one place: init. data class IssuerCall( val url: String, val method: String = "GET", val headers: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(), val timeout: Duration = Duration.ofSeconds(2), val maxRetries: Int = 0, ) { init { // runs for every construction, copy() included require(maxRetries >= 0) { "maxRetries must be >= 0, was $maxRetries" } } } fun main() { val call = IssuerCall( url = "https://issuer.example/authorize", method = "POST", headers = mapOf("Idempotency-Key" to "auth-7731"), maxRetries = 2, ) println("built: $call") println("faster copy: ${call.copy(timeout = Duration.ofMillis(800)).timeout}") // Map is a read-only type, so there is no put(). Force a cast and the map behind it refuses too: val write = runCatching { (call.headers as MutableMap<String, String>)["X-Debug"] = "1" } println("headers: ${if (write.isFailure) "unmodifiable" else "writable!"}") try { call.copy(maxRetries = -1) // copy() can't skip validation either } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("copy(): ${e.message}") } }

try.expect: The first run prints the built call, PT0.8S for the faster copy, headers: unmodifiable and wither: maxRetries must be >= 0, was -1. With .maxRetries(-1) the program dies in build(), and the stack trace points into the record's compact constructor: the builder has no rules of its own, so it can't forget any. The Kotlin twin fails in the same place, its init block, and prints copy(): maxRetries must be >= 0, was -1 for the copy.

sections.h: Type-safe builders: lambdas with receivers and @DslMarker
sections.html:
For nested data, Kotlin lets you write a builder that reads like a configuration file:

Java
// Java has no lambdas with receivers; the closest is a Consumer that receives the builder
PaymentRequest req = paymentRequest(r -> {
    r.idempotencyKey("order-981-attempt-1");
    r.lineItems(items -> {
        items.item("sku-1", 1_000);
        items.item("sku-2", 500);
    });
    r.metadata("orderId", "981");
});
Kotlin
val req = paymentRequest {
    idempotencyKey = "order-981-attempt-1"
    lineItems {
        item("sku-1", 1_000)
        item("sku-2", 500)
    }
    metadata("orderId", "981")
}

The trick is a lambda with receiver. paymentRequest takes a PaymentRequestBuilder.() -> Unit: a function that runs with a builder as this. Inside the braces, idempotencyKey and lineItems are members of that builder:

Java
static PaymentRequest paymentRequest(Consumer<PaymentRequestBuilder> block) {
    PaymentRequestBuilder b = new PaymentRequestBuilder();
    block.accept(b);                                   // the block gets the builder as a parameter
    return b.build();
}

final class PaymentRequestBuilder {
    private String idempotencyKey;
    private final List<LineItem> items = new ArrayList<>();
    void idempotencyKey(String key) { idempotencyKey = key; }
    void lineItems(Consumer<LineItemsBuilder> block) {
        LineItemsBuilder b = new LineItemsBuilder();
        block.accept(b);
        items.addAll(b.build());
    }
    PaymentRequest build() { /* validate, then copy into the request */ }
}
Kotlin
fun paymentRequest(block: PaymentRequestBuilder.() -> Unit): PaymentRequest =
    PaymentRequestBuilder().apply(block).build()

class PaymentRequestBuilder {
    var idempotencyKey: String? = null
    private val items = mutableListOf<LineItem>()
    fun lineItems(block: LineItemsBuilder.() -> Unit) { items += LineItemsBuilder().apply(block).build() }
    fun build(): PaymentRequest { /* validate, then copy into the request */ }
}

Gradle's Kotlin DSL, Ktor routing and kotlinx.html are built the same way. The Java shape, a Consumer per block, is what Spring Security's lambda configuration uses. The builder is still a builder: build() is the one place that sees every field, so it validates there.

There is one trap. Inside lineItems { }, two receivers are in scope: the LineItemsBuilder and the outer PaymentRequestBuilder. So idempotencyKey = "x" written inside the inner block compiles and quietly sets the outer field. @DslMarker closes that hole:

Java
// Java needs no marker: each block names its builder, so reaching the outer one means typing r
r.lineItems(items -> {
    items.item("sku-1", 1_000);
    r.idempotencyKey("x");       // compiles, but you can see it in review
});
Kotlin
@DslMarker annotation class PaymentDsl

@PaymentDsl class PaymentRequestBuilder { ... }
@PaymentDsl class LineItemsBuilder { ... }

With both builders marked, the compiler only lets you call members of the nearest receiver without a prefix. Reaching the outer one needs an explicit label, this@paymentRequest.idempotencyKey, which nobody writes by accident.

Build a DSL only when the data nests. A flat request with seven fields is clearer with named arguments, and a DSL would add two classes and a layer of indirection for nothing. The payoff comes with structure: line items under a payment, split payouts under a marketplace order, routing rules under a merchant. It also helps when many people write the same kind of configuration, because inside each block the IDE offers only that builder's methods.

try.title: Make the inner block reach outside
steps: Uncomment the line reason = "oops" inside the refunds { } block. Predict, then run.
Now delete both @RefundDsl lines above the two builder classes (keep the annotation class itself) and run again. What is the batch's reason?
Restore the file. Then open the Java twin and uncomment batchB.reason("oops"): it compiles, but notice that you had to type the outer builder's name.

code.title: DslScope.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l03 // A tiny refund-batch DSL. @DslMarker stops an inner block from reaching the outer builder by accident. @DslMarker annotation class RefundDsl data class Refund(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long) data class RefundBatch(val reason: String, val refunds: List<Refund>) @RefundDsl class RefundsBuilder { private val refunds = mutableListOf<Refund>() fun refund(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long) { refunds += Refund(paymentId, amountMinor) } fun build() = refunds.toList() } @RefundDsl class RefundBatchBuilder { var reason: String = "unspecified" private var refunds: List<Refund> = emptyList() fun refunds(block: RefundsBuilder.() -> Unit) { refunds = RefundsBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun build() = RefundBatch(reason, refunds) } fun refundBatch(block: RefundBatchBuilder.() -> Unit): RefundBatch = RefundBatchBuilder().apply(block).build() fun main() { val batch = refundBatch { reason = "duplicate charge" refunds { refund("p-101", 1_250) refund("p-102", 990) // reason = "oops" // step 2 of the Try it: uncomment this line } } println(batch) println("total refunded: ${batch.refunds.sumOf { it.amountMinor }}") }

alt.title: DslScopeJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** * The Java twin of DslScope.kt. Java has no lambdas with receivers, so each block is a Consumer * that gets its builder as a named parameter (the style Spring Security uses for its config DSL). */ public class DslScopeJava { record Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor) {} record RefundBatch(String reason, List<Refund> refunds) {} static final class RefundsBuilder { private final List<Refund> refunds = new ArrayList<>(); RefundsBuilder refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor) { refunds.add(new Refund(paymentId, amountMinor)); return this; } List<Refund> build() { return List.copyOf(refunds); } } static final class RefundBatchBuilder { private String reason = "unspecified"; private List<Refund> refunds = List.of(); RefundBatchBuilder reason(String r) { reason = r; return this; } RefundBatchBuilder refunds(Consumer<RefundsBuilder> block) { RefundsBuilder b = new RefundsBuilder(); block.accept(b); refunds = b.build(); return this; } RefundBatch build() { return new RefundBatch(reason, refunds); } } static RefundBatch refundBatch(Consumer<RefundBatchBuilder> block) { RefundBatchBuilder b = new RefundBatchBuilder(); block.accept(b); return b.build(); } public static void main(String[] args) { RefundBatch batch = refundBatch(batchB -> { batchB.reason("duplicate charge"); batchB.refunds(r -> { r.refund("p-101", 1_250); r.refund("p-102", 990); // batchB.reason("oops"); // step 2 of the Try it: this compiles, but you have to name batchB }); }); System.out.println(batch); System.out.println("total refunded: " + batch.refunds().stream().mapToLong(Refund::amountMinor).sum()); } }

try.expect: The first run prints a batch with reason duplicate charge and total refunded: 2240. With the line uncommented, the build fails: 'var reason: String' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. Without the marker it compiles and prints reason=oops: the inner block silently rewrote the outer batch.

sections.h: Prototype: every copy is shallow until you make it deep
sections.html:
Prototype means making a new object by copying an existing one and changing a few fields. Payment code does this constantly: a recurring-charge template copied per merchant, a default config copied per tenant, a test fixture copied per test.

Java's original mechanism, Cloneable, is broken by design. The interface has no clone method, so implementing it gives callers nothing to call. Object.clone() is protected and makes a shallow copy. To use it you override clone, call super.clone(), catch a CloneNotSupportedException that can't happen, and then fix every mutable field by hand. Skip it. Use a copy constructor, a static copy factory, or a wither on a record.

Records make withers easy to write and Kotlin data classes generate copy(). Neither copies deeply. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: copy() creates a shallow copy, and references to other objects are shared.

Java
record Cart(String id, List<String> skus) {
    Cart withId(String newId) { return new Cart(newId, skus); }   // a wither: shares the list
}
var c1 = new Cart("c1", new ArrayList<>(List.of("sku-1")));
var c2 = c1.withId("c2");
c2.skus().add("sku-2");     // c1.skus() is now [sku-1, sku-2]
Kotlin
data class Cart(val id: String, val skus: MutableList<String>)
val c1 = Cart("c1", mutableListOf("sku-1"))
val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2")
c2.skus += "sku-2"          // c1.skus is now [sku-1, sku-2]

The fix is the same in both languages. Store collections you can't change (List.copyOf in a compact constructor in Java; a read-only List in Kotlin), and let withers build a new collection: copy(skus = skus + "sku-2").

Kotlin has a second trap. data class Email private constructor(val value: String) still gets a public copy(), so Email.of("anna@example.com").copy(value = "not-an-email") compiles and skips your factory. Kotlin 2.4 only warns, and the warning says it becomes an error in language version 2.5. Add @ConsistentCopyVisibility to make copy() as private as the constructor in the current release. Validation in an init block is safer still, because copy() runs it. Java records never had the private-constructor illusion: a record's canonical constructor can't be less visible than the record, so the rules belong in the compact constructor from the start.

try.title: Spring both copy traps
steps: Read CopyTrap.kt (or its Java twin) and predict the three lines it prints.
Run it. If Gradle recompiles the file, read the w: warnings too.
Add @ConsistentCopyVisibility on the line above data class Email and run again.

code.title: CopyTrap.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l03 // Two traps in data class copy(): it is shallow, and it ignores a private constructor. data class Cart(val id: String, val skus: MutableList<String>) data class Email private constructor(val value: String) { companion object { fun of(raw: String): Email { require("@" in raw) { "not an email: $raw" } return Email(raw) } } } data class Amount(val minor: Long) { init { require(minor >= 0) { "negative amount: $minor" } } } fun main() { // trap 1: copy() copies the reference to the list, not the list val c1 = Cart("c1", mutableListOf("sku-1")) val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2") c2.skus += "sku-2" println("c1.skus after changing c2: ${c1.skus}") // trap 2: the private constructor does not cover the generated copy() val email = Email.of("anna@example.com") val broken = email.copy(value = "not-an-email") println("copy() skipped the factory: $broken") // init blocks DO run on copy() val result = runCatching { Amount(5).copy(minor = -1) } println("Amount(5).copy(minor = -1): ${result.exceptionOrNull()?.message}") }

alt.title: CopyTrapJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** The Java twin of CopyTrap.kt: record copies are shallow, and a factory can't hide a record's constructor. */ public class CopyTrapJava { record Cart(String id, List<String> skus) { Cart withId(String newId) { return new Cart(newId, skus); } // a hand-written wither: shares the list } record Email(String value) { // a record's canonical constructor is never more private than the record itself, // so this factory can always be bypassed with new Email(...) static Email of(String raw) { if (!raw.contains("@")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("not an email: " + raw); return new Email(raw); } } record Amount(long minor) { Amount { // compact constructor: every path runs it if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + minor); } Amount withMinor(long m) { return new Amount(m); } } public static void main(String[] args) { // trap 1: the wither copies the reference to the list, not the list Cart c1 = new Cart("c1", new ArrayList<>(List.of("sku-1"))); Cart c2 = c1.withId("c2"); c2.skus().add("sku-2"); System.out.println("c1.skus after changing c2: " + c1.skus()); // trap 2: the factory validates, the canonical constructor doesn't Email broken = new Email("not-an-email"); System.out.println("new skipped the factory: " + broken); // the compact constructor DOES run on withers try { new Amount(5).withMinor(-1); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("new Amount(5).withMinor(-1): " + e.getMessage()); } } }

try.expect: It prints c1.skus after changing c2: [sku-1, sku-2] (the copy shared the list), copy() skipped the factory: Email(value=not-an-email), and negative amount: -1, because init runs on copy(). The compiler warns that the non-public primary constructor is exposed via copy(). With @ConsistentCopyVisibility, the build stops with Cannot access 'fun copy(value: String = ...): Email': it is private. The Java twin prints the same story: the wither shares the list, new Email("not-an-email") skips the factory, and the compact constructor rejects -1.

analogy: A builder is an order form at a card-printing desk: you tick the boxes you care about, leave the rest at their defaults, and the clerk checks the whole form before printing anything. Kotlin's named arguments are a form so short you fill it in at the counter. Prototype is photocopying a filled-in form and changing two fields. The analogy breaks on the shallow copy: a photocopy is a real, separate piece of paper, while copy() gives you a new form that still points at the same attached sheet of line items, so writing on the copy's attachment writes on the original's.
world: Payment requests to an issuer have a dozen optional fields: descriptor, 3-D Secure data, metadata, capture mode, retry policy. In Kotlin services, a data class with defaults and an init block is all you need. For a shared client library that Java services call, add a builder. Test fixtures are prototypes: one baseAuthorization copied per test with copy(amountMinor = 0). If that fixture holds a MutableList of line items, one test can poison every test after it. The same goes for a Quarkus @ApplicationScoped bean that hands out a default config object which callers then copy and modify.
mistake: The most common mistake is trusting copy() or a record wither to make an independent object when a component is mutable. A MutableList, a HashMap, an array or a mutable Date is shared between the original and the copy, so changing one changes both. It happens because the class looks immutable: every property is val, or it's a record. The fix is to store copies that can't change (List.copyOf in a compact constructor, read-only types and toList() in Kotlin), and to make withers build new collections instead of mutating the shared one.

compare.title: A prototype that copies safely

java.title: TenantConfig.java
java.html: record TenantConfig(String tenantId, List<String> paymentMethods, Map<String, Long> dailyLimits) { TenantConfig { // every copy passes through here paymentMethods = List.copyOf(paymentMethods); dailyLimits = Map.copyOf(dailyLimits); } TenantConfig forTenant(String id) { // safe to share: nothing can change return new TenantConfig(id, paymentMethods, dailyLimits); } TenantConfig withMethod(String method) { // copy, change the copy, wrap again var methods = new ArrayList<>(paymentMethods); methods.add(method); return new TenantConfig(tenantId, methods, dailyLimits); } } var base = new TenantConfig("default", List.of("CARD"), Map.of("CARD", 500_000L)); var acme = base.forTenant("acme").withMethod("SEPA");

kotlin.title: TenantConfig.kt
kotlin.html: data class TenantConfig( val tenantId: String, val paymentMethods: List<String>, // read-only types val dailyLimits: Map<String, Long>, ) val base = TenantConfig("default", listOf("CARD"), mapOf("CARD" to 500_000L)) val acme = base.copy( tenantId = "acme", paymentMethods = base.paymentMethods + "SEPA", // + builds a new list )

compare.note: Kotlin generates copy() with named arguments, so it needs no withers, and + on a read-only List or Map returns a new collection. Java needs one hand-written wither per field. Both copies are shallow, and the safety comes from the components, not from the copy. There is one real difference: Java's compact constructor can replace the incoming list with List.copyOf, while a Kotlin data class property can't be reassigned in init. A Kotlin List parameter is only read-only, so a caller who passes a MutableList and keeps a reference can still change it. If that matters, take the list as a plain constructor parameter and store toList() in a property.

worked.title: From a telescoping constructor to a record and builder, and to a Kotlin class

steps.say: Here is a call to an issuer charge request with eight positional arguments. Before reading on, say which argument is the statement descriptor, and which rule you'd expect ChargeRequest to enforce.
steps.code: new ChargeRequest(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42", "ACME*ORDER 981", null, true, 2, 30_000);

alt.html: ChargeRequest(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42", "ACME*ORDER 981", null, true, 2, 30_000)

steps.say: Put every rule in one place that all paths go through: the record's compact constructor in Java, the init block in Kotlin. The cross-field rule (a descriptor only on captured charges, and 22 characters at most) can only be checked where all fields are known. Kotlin also gets its defaults here, which is half of what a builder does.
steps.code: record ChargeRequest(long amountMinor, String currency, String token, String descriptor, String threeDsData, boolean capture, int maxRetries, long timeoutMs) { ChargeRequest { if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive"); // 1. single-field rules if (maxRetries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("maxRetries must be >= 0"); if (descriptor != null && (!capture || descriptor.length() > 22)) // 2. cross-field rule throw new IllegalArgumentException("descriptor needs capture=true and at most 22 chars"); } }

alt.html: data class ChargeRequest @JvmOverloads constructor( val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String, val token: String, val descriptor: String? = null, // 3. defaults live in the signature val threeDsData: String? = null, val capture: Boolean = true, val maxRetries: Int = 0, val timeoutMs: Long = 10_000, ) { init { require(amountMinor > 0) { "amount must be positive" } // 1. single-field rules require(maxRetries >= 0) { "maxRetries must be >= 0" } require(descriptor == null || (capture && descriptor.length <= 22)) { // 2. cross-field rule "descriptor needs capture=true and at most 22 chars" } } }

steps.say: Java needs a builder that only collects and supplies defaults; its build() calls the canonical constructor, so the rules run there. Kotlin needs no builder: named arguments do the job, and @JvmOverloads gives Java callers some overloads. If Java teams call the Kotlin class often, add a builder for them too.
steps.code: static final class Builder { private final long amountMinor; private final String currency; private final String token; private String descriptor; private String threeDsData; private boolean capture = true; private int maxRetries = 0; private long timeoutMs = 10_000; // 3. defaults Builder(long amountMinor, String currency, String token) { this.amountMinor = amountMinor; this.currency = currency; this.token = token; // 4. required up front } Builder descriptor(String d) { descriptor = d; return this; } Builder maxRetries(int n) { maxRetries = n; return this; } Builder timeoutMs(long ms) { timeoutMs = ms; return this; } ChargeRequest build() { return new ChargeRequest(amountMinor, currency, token, descriptor, threeDsData, capture, maxRetries, timeoutMs); } } var req = new ChargeRequest.Builder(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42").descriptor("ACME*ORDER 981").maxRetries(2).build();

drill.title: A two-level DSL from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write fun refundBatch(block: RefundBatchBuilder.() -> Unit): RefundBatch, where the builder has a var reason and a nested refunds { refund(paymentId, amountMinor) } block, and @DslMarker stops the inner block from setting reason. Then compare with the answer, and with the Java twin built from Consumers.

answer.html: @DslMarker annotation class RefundDsl data class Refund(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long) data class RefundBatch(val reason: String, val refunds: List<Refund>) @RefundDsl class RefundsBuilder { private val refunds = mutableListOf<Refund>() fun refund(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long) { refunds += Refund(paymentId, amountMinor) } fun build() = refunds.toList() } @RefundDsl class RefundBatchBuilder { var reason: String = "unspecified" private var refunds: List<Refund> = emptyList() fun refunds(block: RefundsBuilder.() -> Unit) { refunds = RefundsBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun build() = RefundBatch(reason, refunds) } fun refundBatch(block: RefundBatchBuilder.() -> Unit): RefundBatch = RefundBatchBuilder().apply(block).build()

alt.title: Java
alt.html: // Java has no lambdas with receivers: each block is a Consumer of its builder record Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor) {} record RefundBatch(String reason, List<Refund> refunds) {} final class RefundsBuilder { private final List<Refund> refunds = new ArrayList<>(); void refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor) { refunds.add(new Refund(paymentId, amountMinor)); } List<Refund> build() { return List.copyOf(refunds); } } final class RefundBatchBuilder { private String reason = "unspecified"; private List<Refund> refunds = List.of(); void reason(String r) { reason = r; } void refunds(Consumer<RefundsBuilder> block) { RefundsBuilder b = new RefundsBuilder(); block.accept(b); refunds = b.build(); } RefundBatch build() { return new RefundBatch(reason, refunds); } } static RefundBatch refundBatch(Consumer<RefundBatchBuilder> block) { RefundBatchBuilder b = new RefundBatchBuilder(); block.accept(b); return b.build(); }

recap: Kotlin named and default arguments, plus copy(), replace most builders. Put validation in init: it runs for every construction, copy() included.
A builder still helps for Java callers, for construction spread over several steps, and for nested data. In Java, pair a validating record (compact constructor) with a builder that only collects.
A type-safe DSL is a function that takes a lambda with receiver (Builder.() -> Unit). @DslMarker stops an inner block from silently reaching an outer builder.
Cloneable has no clone method and Object.clone() is shallow. Use copy constructors, copy factories or withers.
Record withers and data class copy() are shallow. Store collections that can't change, and build new collections in withers.
In Kotlin 2.4 a private constructor doesn't make copy() private. Add @ConsistentCopyVisibility, or rely on init checks, which copy() runs.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "Kotlin data classes are immutable, so copy() gives us safe, independent templates." Explain where that's wrong, and how you'd make templates safe in Kotlin and in Java.
explain.answer: Data classes are only as immutable as their properties. val stops a property from pointing somewhere else, but if it holds a MutableList or a HashMap, copy() copies the reference, so the template and every copy share that collection, and changing one changes all of them. To make templates safe, give them collections that can't change: in Kotlin, read-only List and Map types and copy(items = items + x) to build new ones; in Java, a record whose compact constructor stores List.copyOf and Map.copyOf, and withers that copy, change the copy and construct a new record. I'd also put the rules in init or the compact constructor, because copy() and withers go through them.

deeper.html:
Effective Java's hierarchical builder solves a problem you may meet in a shared Java library: a Pizza.Builder that subclasses (NyPizza.Builder, Calzone.Builder) extend without losing the subclass type in a chain. It uses a recursive type parameter, Builder<T extends Builder<T>>, and an abstract self() method that each subclass implements as return this;. The generics track explains why that recursive bound works. In Kotlin you almost never need it, because named arguments and copy() remove the chain.

Java has no with syntax for records yet. Project Amber has proposed one, derived record creation (JEP 468), where you would write something like point with { x = 3; }. Check its status on the JEP page before you plan around it. Until then, write withers for the fields that really change.

People sometimes deep-copy an object graph by serializing and deserializing it, or with a reflection library. It works, it is slow, and it copies things you didn't mean to copy, such as a shared Clock or a connection. If you need a deep copy, the cleaner fix is usually to make the components immutable so a shallow copy is enough.

Kotlin's buildList { add(...) }, buildMap { } and buildString { } are small standard-library builders with receivers. Use them when you build a collection with loops or conditions; the result is read-only once the block returns.
